judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's mathematics is correct throughout and I could not fault a single value. Problem 1's limit of (4n+1)/(n+7) is 4, so the nth-term test proves divergence; problem 2's limit of 1/sqrt(n) is 0, which licenses nothing, and the p-series test with p = 1/2 <= 1 settles it as divergent; problem 3 is sum 2(1/3)^n from n = 0, which is 2/(1 - 1/3) = 3, with the declared trap 6 = 2/(1/3) reproducing the 'divided by the ratio instead of by one minus the ratio' slip exactly; problem 4 telescopes to 1; problem 5's two ratio limits are both exactly 1; problem 6's endpoints from c = 2 and r = 3 are -1 and 5; problem 7's alternating harmonic sum is -ln 2 because the first term is negative, giving the interval [-1, 5). Eight problems, multiple explicit inconclusive-test and omitted-endpoint traps, and a study guide that states the logical scope of each test. The one thing 32/32 does not survive is how the sheet's written demands are classified. The directions box says 'For every problem, name the test you used and say exactly what it licenses', and problem 5 is even labelled on the worksheet '(Open response - your teacher checks part (b))' with a matching {"type":"manual"} entry - proving the mechanism was in hand. Yet five other problems make demands of exactly the same kind with no manual companion: problem 1 'state what the nth-term test lets you conclude', problem 2 'state precisely what the nth-term test does and does not license here, and name the test that actually settles this series - together with its verdict', problem 3 'Identify the formula the student misremembered', problem 6 'A student who reports one endpoint as 3 has made a specific mistake - name it', problem 7 'state whether the left endpoint belongs to the interval of convergence ... say why the sum must be negative'. Problem 2 is the sharpest case: the student is TOLD Devi's limit is correct, so the verified entry (limit = 0) is the half of the item that is given, and the unverified half - p = 1/2 <= 1 therefore the p-series diverges - is the entire point of the problem. The same class of demand is classified two different ways inside one verify.json. Minor: the bank prints '7. - log(2)' where the worksheet and key write ln 2, via render_quick_answers._fmt's sympify/latex round trip.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 2's construction is the cleanest statement of the target misconception in this batch: Devi's LIMIT is correct and only her inference is wrong. The item cannot be solved by recomputing, which is precisely what an inconclusive-test error demands - the student has to say what the nth-term test licenses, not what the limit equals. Building the item so that the computable part is conceded is the right design for this instructional mode.

Problem 5 gives two series that both return a ratio-test limit of exactly 1 - the harmonic series with ratio n/(n+1) and the reciprocal squares with ratio n^2/(n+1)^2 - verifies BOTH limits as 1 (ids 5), and then asks why a limit of 1 can never be evidence either way. The proof that the test is uninformative is delivered as two machine-checked identical limits with opposite outcomes, which is far stronger than asserting inconclusiveness.

Each of the four declared traps maps onto a named reasoning slip rather than an arithmetic slip, and the key prints the diagnosis beside the number: 6 for dividing by the ratio instead of one minus the ratio, 0.5 for reporting the first term as the whole sum, 3 for giving the radius itself as an endpoint, and 0.693 for keeping an alternating sum positive when its first term is negative. That last one is the exact error problem 7 asks the student to explain.

root_causes.description: Five problems print an explicit written-diagnosis slot with no manual companion, while problem 5 carries one under the same file. The sheet's own directions require a named test and a statement of what it licenses on every problem, so the verified entries cover the computational halves and the assessed halves ship as though machine-checked.

improvements.title: Five named-diagnosis slots (problems 1, 2, 3, 6, 7) ship without manual companions while problem 5 has one
improvements.proposed_change: Make the manual companion automatic rather than discretionary. Trigger on stem phrases 'state what ... lets you conclude', 'state precisely what ... licenses', 'identify the formula', 'name it', 'name the test', 'say why', and have verify.py refuse to report a fully machine-verified id when its stem contains one. On this sheet that raises the manual count from 2 to 7 and, more importantly, puts problem 2's p-series verdict - the item's whole content, since its limit is conceded in the stem - in front of a human reader. Also carry through to final_response.md, which should list the open items rather than summarise them as one.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: a stem reading 'Compute the limit yourself, state precisely what the nth-term test does and does not license here, and name the test that actually settles this series' with only a limit entry under that id. verify.py must exit non-zero requesting the manual companion. Adding the manual entry passes, and a control fixture whose stem is purely computational must still pass with no manual entry. The failing fixture passes today.
improvements.expected_impact: In misconception-analysis mode, where the named diagnosis IS the assessed skill, the manual-review list stops understating the sheet by a factor of three, and no diagnosis is delivered under the claim of machine verification.
improvements.risk: Low to medium. The phrase list must stay tight or routine 'show your work' stems will inflate manual counts; fixture-locking the list keeps that bounded. Build exit codes move from 0 to 2 on some sheets, which the harness already handles.

case_summary: The most precisely targeted sheet in my batch. Every problem attacks a logical error rather than an algebraic one: problem 1 establishes that a non-zero limit proves divergence, problem 2 concedes that Devi's limit is right so only her inference can be graded, problem 5 verifies two ratio-test limits that are both exactly 1 on series with opposite outcomes, and problems 6 through 8 walk the omitted-endpoint error from 'the radius is not an endpoint' to the full interval [-1, 5) with the correct bracket at each end. I recomputed all eleven verified quantities - the limits 4, 0, 1, 1, the sums 3 and 1, the endpoints -1 and 5, and the left-endpoint sum -ln 2 - and every one is correct, as are the four declared traps, each of which maps onto a named reasoning slip. The gap the judge missed is in classification, not content: problem 5 is explicitly labelled open response and carries a manual entry, yet problems 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7 make demands of exactly the same kind - 'state what the test lets you conclude', 'name the test that actually settles this series', 'identify the formula the student misremembered', 'name it', 'say why the sum must be negative' - with no manual companion. On problem 2 that means the verified half is the half the worksheet already gives away, and the half that carries the whole item ships unread.
